title: Short Stuff: The Guinness Widget
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Guinness widget, the small hollow plastic sphere inside cans of Guinness. The hosts cover the widget's name origin (a 1924 play, with Guinness later patenting the term), how Michael Ash and John Lunn's work led to nitrogen-infused canned Guinness that mimics cask-poured beer, the widget's mechanics (nitrogen-filled sphere with a hole that jets beer and gas out on opening, creating a creamy cascade head), the 1969 patent (Project Oak Tree), the switch to a floating widget in 1997, the 2004 poll ranking it above the Internet, and other brands using widgets. Also includes banter about pub Guinness, the surge-and-settle pour, cream stouts, and the Nitro Surge device. Includes an ad read for Banquet Beer.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Guinness widget topic and chat about a listener suggestion from Brian Didsbury.

segments.title: Widget name origin
segments.summary: The word widget is thought to have come from a 1924 play about being in the widget business; Guinness later made the term a patented name for its device.

segments.title: What the widget is
segments.summary: Describes the small plastic sphere with a hole found inside a can of Guinness, which the company calls a smooth.

segments.title: Michael Ash and carbonation problem
segments.summary: Michael Ash, a master brewer who joined Guinness in 1951, found CO2 made cask-style Guinness fizzy rather than smooth, and cask beer's pour differed because it had to be pumped out of the cask.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before returning to the nitrogen discussion.

segments.title: Nitrogen and the cask-like pour
segments.summary: Nitrogen forms smaller, more stable bubbles and creates a creamier head that replicates cask-poured Guinness; John Lunn, a master distiller, is credited with creating the widget.

segments.title: Patent and Project Oak Tree
segments.summary: Guinness filed a patent in 1969 for dispensing carbonated liquids from containers; the project was renamed from Project Dynamite to Project Oak Tree for customs reasons.

segments.title: Bottle versus pub Guinness and the surge-and-settle pour
segments.summary: Hosts compare canned Guinness with pub and bottled versions, describe the surge-and-settle cascade pour, and briefly mention the Nitro Surge device.

segments.title: How the widget works
segments.summary: The sphere is dropped in before the can is sealed and fills with nitrogen-infused beer; when opened, pressure forces beer out of the hole, agitating the beer and creating bubbles.

segments.title: 2004 poll and cream stouts
segments.summary: A 2004 survey of nearly nine thousand people voted the Guinness widget a greater invention than the Internet; hosts discuss cream stouts and how they feel in the stomach.

segments.title: Floating widget history
segments.summary: Guinness has used a floating widget since 1997; earlier cans had it fixed to the bottom, and during COVID supply issues it was fixed to the bottom again.

segments.title: Other beers using widgets
segments.summary: Hosts list other brands using widget technology, including Old Speckled Hen, Boddingtons, Murphy's, Beamish, Tetley's and Wexford, Kilkenny-style pub drafts.

segments.title: Sponsor read and sign-off
segments.summary: Banquet Beer sponsor mention, followed by the closing credits and iHeartRadio production note.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Closing credits for Short Stuff and Stuff You Should Know.
